summary:
**Earth Jukebox – Turning Earth's Colours into Music**

Earth Jukebox is an interactive web-based project that transforms images of our planet into music, helping people experience Earth's environmental patterns through sound. Using NASA Earth visualizations and uploaded images, the system analyses RGB colour values and converts them into musical elements such as melody, harmony, and bass. It also features a rotating 3D Earth, a live audio waveform visualizer, and interactive music controls.

The project explores how data sonification can make environmental information more accessible, particularly for people who are blind or visually impaired. By combining sound with clear spoken explanations, Earth Jukebox aims to help users understand environmental changes in a more engaging, non-visual way.

This project is important because climate change affects everyone, and understanding our planet should not depend on the ability to see. It brings creativity, technology, accessibility, and environmental awareness together.
details:
Earth Jukebox – Experience Earth Through Music

Earth Jukebox is an interactive web-based project that transforms Earth's images into original musical experiences. Users can select climate, ocean, and forest images or upload their own JPG, PNG, or WEBP images. The system analyses the average RGB pixel values and maps them to musical notes, generating melody, harmony, and bass using a digital audio engine. Users can control playback, volume, and tempo while viewing a live waveform. The website also features a rotating 3D Earth and an accessibility mode with spoken page guidance and voice navigation.

The project aims to make Earth-related visual information more engaging and accessible, especially for people who are blind or visually impaired. Its creative approach combines image processing, music generation, 3D visualization, and speech technology in one interactive experience.

I developed the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for the 3D Earth and Tone.js for music generation. I also used browser speech technologies, Canvas for image analysis and waveform visualization, Sublime Text for coding, and a web browser for testing. No special hardware is required, although a microphone is needed for voice navigation.

Key factors considered include accessibility, ease of use, responsive design, browser compatibility, user privacy, and scientific accuracy. The current RGB-to-music feature is an artistic representation of image colours, not a direct measurement of climate data. Future development will integrate documented NASA numerical datasets and spoken climate explanations to support a more scientifically grounded audio experience.
